title: Why We Need to Eat

before.title: Why We Need to Eat
before.text:
Every single day, our bodies require food to provide the energy necessary for countless key activities, from simply breathing and thinking to running, playing, and growing properly.

When we eat food, our digestive system breaks it down into smaller, simpler substances our bodies can actually use. This process begins in our mouth, where chewing breaks food into smaller pieces.

After swallowing, food travels down to our stomach, where powerful acids and enzymes continue breaking it down further into a liquid mixture. This mixture then moves into our small intestine.

Within the small intestine, food from our food, including proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals, are absorbed directly into our bloodstream, traveling throughout our entire body.

These essential food provide energy for our muscles, help our brain think clearly, support healthy bone and muscle growth, and help our immune system fight off harmful germs and illness.

Different foods provide different key food, which explains why eating a balanced variety of foods, including fruits, vegetables, grains, and proteins, helps keep our bodies healthy and functioning properly.

Without regularly eating nutritious food, our bodies would quickly run out of necessary energy. This made it hard to perform even simple daily activities, emphasizing just how essential proper nutrition truly is for maintaining good overall health.

after.title: Why We Need to Eat
after.text:
Our bodies need nutrients from food and drink to work properly and stay healthy. Nutrients help provide energy and support growth and cell repair.

Digestion breaks food into parts small enough for the body to absorb. It begins in the mouth. Chewing cuts food into smaller pieces, and saliva moistens it. An enzyme in saliva also begins to break down starch.

After we swallow, muscles push food through the esophagus to the stomach. The stomach mixes it with acid and enzymes. The partly digested mixture then enters the small intestine.

Digestive juices from the pancreas, liver and small intestine help break down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. The wall of the small intestine absorbs most nutrients. Many pass into the bloodstream, while the lymph system absorbs fatty acids and some vitamins.

The blood carries absorbed nutrients to the liver and other parts of the body. The body can use simple sugars, amino acids and fatty acids to make energy or build and repair cells.

Food also supplies vitamins, minerals and water. No single food supplies everything in the same amounts, so eating a variety of nutritious foods helps us obtain the nutrients our bodies need.

reason: The original contains agreement errors (“food ... are,” “These essential food provide”), repetition (“food from our food”), an incorrect shift to past tense, and oversimplifies absorption. Rewrite the complete explanation to match NIDDK’s account of digestion, nutrient absorption and the uses of nutrients.

title: The Shared Garden

before.title: The Shared Garden
before.text:
This is a made-up policy example based on choices real communities may face.

In a crowded city neighborhood where most families lived in small apartments without private outdoor space, residents chose to transform an empty lot into a shared community garden where all the people could grow vegetables and flowers.

Organizing this needed cooperation. Neighbors needed to agree on rules for dividing plots fairly, maintaining shared tools, and watering plants during hot summer weeks.

After some disagreements, residents established clear guidelines most families felt comfortable following. The garden slowly flourished, providing fresh vegetables and welcome shared green space.

Beyond practical benefits, neighbors reported feeling much more connected, having developed new friendships through their regular, cooperative gardening activities.

after.title: The Shared Garden
after.text:
This is a fictional policy example.

An empty lot stood between two apartment buildings in a crowded neighborhood. Some residents wanted to turn it into a shared garden. Others worried about cost, noise and who would receive the best plots.

At an open meeting, the group listed the choices. They could divide the land into private plots, grow everything together, or use part of the lot as a sitting area. They also needed rules for water, tools and access.

The residents chose a one-year trial. Half the lot held small plots assigned by a lottery. The rest had shared herbs, benches and a path. Members paid a small fee, but anyone could use the sitting area. A volunteer schedule covered watering and cleanup.

After six months, the group reviewed the project. The garden had produced vegetables and a useful green space, but the watering schedule was uneven. The residents decided to add a rain tank and ask the city for advice before beginning a second year.

reason: The passage explicitly identifies itself as a made-up policy example, so explanatory-nonfiction is the wrong classification. Rewrite the generic claims as a concrete fictional scenario, keep the policy trade-offs visible, and avoid presenting invented resident reports as evidence.

title: Jim Finds the Treasure Map

before.title: Jim Finds the Treasure Map
before.text:
Jim Hawkins lived with his parents at a small inn near the sea.

One winter, an old sailor arrived. He carried a heavy sea chest and watched the road carefully.

The sailor stayed for many weeks. He often drank too much and told frightening stories about pirates and storms.

Jim noticed that the man seemed afraid of someone.

One day, another sailor came to the inn. Soon after their meeting, the old sailor died.

Jim and his mother knew that money was owed to them, so they opened the sea chest.

Inside they found coins, clothes, papers, and a small package wrapped in cloth.

Jim took the package.

Later, he opened it with two trusted men from the area.

Inside was a map of an island.

Several places were marked on it, and one mark was especially important. Beside it were words showing where Captain Flint, a famous pirate, had hidden his treasure.

The men looked at one another.

The map could lead to great wealth, but it could also bring danger.

Jim felt both excited and afraid.

Before that night, pirates had been only characters in sailors’ stories. Now Jim was holding a real treasure map in his own hands.

after.title: Jim Finds the Treasure Map
after.text:
Jim Hawkins lived with his parents at the Admiral Benbow inn. An old sailor called Billy Bones stayed there with a heavy sea chest. He drank too much, told frightening stories and watched for other sailors.

One day, a blind man came to the inn and placed a black spot in Billy's hand. It was a warning from his former shipmates. Soon afterward, Billy fell to the floor and died.

Jim and his mother knew that Billy owed them money. They opened his chest and counted only the amount that was due. Jim also took an oilskin packet. Then a whistle warned them that the pirates were coming, so they fled.

Revenue officers later carried Jim to the house where Dr. Livesey and Squire Trelawney were dining. Jim gave the packet to the doctor.

When they opened it, they found an account book and a sealed paper. The paper contained a map of an island. Three red crosses marked places on it, and words beside one cross showed where Captain Flint had hidden most of his treasure.

The squire wanted to find a ship and sail for the island. Dr. Livesey agreed, but warned him to keep the discovery secret. The pirates were still searching for the map.

reason: Compare the complete retelling with Treasure Island, Chapters III–VI. Correct the sequence: the blind man gives Billy Bones the black spot, Billy dies; Jim and his mother take only the debt and oilskin packet before the pirates arrive; Dr. Livesey and Squire Trelawney later open the packet and find an account book plus the map.
